related_questions.question: How accurate are at home COVID tests?

text_blocks.snippet: At-home COVID-19 tests are generally accurate, but not perfect. They are most accurate when someone is experiencing symptoms or has been exposed to the virus. While they are reliable for detecting positive cases, they can produce false negative results, meaning they may not always detect the virus even when someone is infected.

list.title: False Negatives:
list.snippet: At-home tests are less accurate than molecular tests and may not detect the virus early in an infection or in people without symptoms.

list.title: Repeat Testing:
list.snippet: Due to the possibility of false negatives, it's recommended to repeat testing following a negative result, especially if you have symptoms or have been exposed to someone with COVID-19, according to the FDA.

list.title: When to be Cautious:
list.snippet: UCHealth says if you have symptoms or have been in close contact with someone who tested positive, don't rely solely on a negative at-home test result.

list.title: Positive Results:
list.snippet: A positive at-home test result is generally considered accurate.

list.title: Reporting Results:
list.snippet: The FDA encourages voluntary and anonymous reporting of test results, regardless of whether they are positive or negative.

text_blocks.snippet: At-home COVID tests, specifically antigen tests, are generally accurate when detecting positive results, especially when symptoms are present. However, they are less sensitive at detecting asymptomatic infections. Repeat testing is recommended after a negative result, particularly for those with symptoms or potential exposure, to minimize the risk of false negatives.

list.title: Positive Results are Generally Accurate:
list.snippet: Antigen tests, which are commonly used in at-home tests, are reliable in detecting positive cases, especially when symptoms are present.

list.title: Sensitivity Varies:
list.snippet: At-home tests are less sensitive in detecting early infections or asymptomatic cases. A study in Microbiology Spectrum found that they detected about half of asymptomatic cases compared to almost 90% of symptomatic cases.

list.title: Repeat Testing Recommended:
list.snippet: The FDA recommends repeating at-home antigen tests after a negative result, especially if symptoms persist or exposure is suspected, to reduce the chance of a false negative.

list.title: Symptomatic vs. Asymptomatic:
list.snippet: At-home tests are more effective when someone is experiencing symptoms.

list.title: Molecular Tests More Sensitive:
list.snippet: PCR tests (often done in labs) are generally more sensitive and can detect lower levels of the virus, including early in the infection and in asymptomatic individuals.
